summary: 15 concise trial-paper-only hypotheses distilled from the ResearchAgent run for sprint, grouped by the characteristic each names.

mechanisms.description: Lower baseline eGFR reflects reduced renal reserve and impaired autoregulation so intensive SBP lowering is more likely to convert an early creatinine rise into persistent eGFR loss via ischemic tubular and nephron loss rather than a benign hemodynamic dip.

Higher baseline albuminuria indicates preexisting glomerular barrier injury and glomerulosclerosis, which predisposes patients to progression when perfusion falls with intensive BP lowering and thus magnifies the risk that an early eGFR decline represents intrinsic injury.

Preexisting RAAS blockade reduces efferent arteriolar tone and glomerular filtration pressure, so adding intensive SBP lowering more readily produces a nonreversible drop in GFR through loss of transglomerular pressure rather than a purely functional change.

Baseline loop diuretic therapy promotes intravascular volume contraction and tubular hypoperfusion, increasing the likelihood that intensive SBP lowering causes ischemic tubular injury and persistent creatinine elevation rather than transient hemodynamic reduction.

Presence of orthostatic hypotension signifies impaired systemic and renal autoregulation and episodic hypoperfusion, so intensive BP targets will more frequently translate early eGFR drops into sustained injury through recurrent renal ischemia.

Elevated baseline NT‑proBNP as a marker of cardiac dysfunction and low forward flow predisposes the kidney to perfusion-dependent injury, such that intensive SBP lowering increases risk of persistent eGFR decline driven by reduced renal perfusion pressure.

Anatomic renal artery stenosis creates perfusion dependence on higher systemic pressure, so intensive SBP reduction is more likely to cause frank ischemic loss of filtration and persistent renal dysfunction rather than reversible hemodynamic change.

Increased arterial stiffness blunts dampening of systolic pressure and impairs microvascular autoregulation, making intensive SBP lowering more apt to cause cortical hypoperfusion and tubular injury with persistent eGFR loss.

Advanced age is associated with fewer nephrons and diminished autoregulatory capacity, so older participants are more susceptible to sustained kidney injury from aggressive SBP lowering following an early eGFR decline.

Black race, reflecting differences in hypertension phenotype and higher baseline glomerulosclerosis prevalence in this cohort, may modify response to intensive SBP lowering by increasing risk that an early eGFR fall represents progressive intrinsic kidney disease rather than only hemodynamic change.

Higher baseline systolic BP leads to larger absolute BP reductions with intensification and thus greater acute declines in renal perfusion pressure, increasing the probability that early eGFR drops reflect injurious hypoperfusion rather than benign adjustment.

Underlying coronary artery disease signifies impaired cardiac reserve and episodic low cardiac output states, so intensive BP lowering may more readily precipitate renal hypoperfusion and persistent tubular injury after an early eGFR decline.

Lower baseline hemoglobin reduces renal oxygen delivery and heightens susceptibility to ischemic tubular injury during reductions in renal perfusion caused by intensive SBP lowering, making early eGFR drops more likely to persist.

Regular NSAID exposure impairs prostaglandin‑mediated afferent arteriolar vasodilation and renal autoregulation, so intensive SBP lowering in NSAID users more commonly converts early eGFR declines into intrinsic renal injury and sustained loss.

Higher baseline BMI promotes hyperfiltration and increased intrarenal metabolic demand such that aggressive BP reduction can unmask tubular vulnerability and lead to persistent eGFR decline after an initial drop rather than simple hemodynamic stabilization.
